name: semantic-kernel

facts.description: Integrate cutting-edge LLM technology quickly and easily into your apps

title: Semantic Kernel: Microsoft's SDK for Building LLM-Powered AI Applications
answer: Semantic Kernel is Microsoft's open source SDK, written in C#, for integrating large language models into applications. It sits between your code and AI services such as OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Google, Mistral, Ollama and Hugging Face, handling chat completion, function calling, plugins and vector store connectors. The one thing to know before adopting it: its plugin and function-calling model is powerful but opinionated, and several connectors are still experimental, so production use means tracking preview APIs and version changes.

sections.body: Semantic Kernel is an open source framework from Microsoft, released under the MIT licence and hosted at github.com/microsoft/semantic-kernel, where it has accumulated roughly 28,600 stars and remains actively maintained, with a last push recorded in October 2026. Its primary language is C#, and its official documentation lives on Microsoft Learn. It occupies the orchestration layer of the AI stack, sitting above raw model APIs and below the application itself. Rather than training models, it connects an application to chat completion services, describes functions to those models, invokes them, and manages the back-and-forth conversation. In that sense it is closer to a glue and control layer than to a modelling library, and it is the piece that turns a model endpoint into something an application can actually act through.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The framework is built around chat completion, which the documentation calls the most common AI service added to Semantic Kernel projects and which is useful for chat bots and autonomous agents. Its strongest ground is function calling. Semantic Kernel serializes available functions and their parameters using JSON schema, sends them with the chat history, extracts function names and arguments from the model's response, invokes the matching code, and returns results to the model until a final message or an iteration limit is reached. Plugins extend this to real work: retrieving data for retrieval augmented generation, automating tasks, and wrapping existing APIs through native code, OpenAPI specifications, or an MCP server. It also covers vector store connectors for data work, with serialization between data models and database schemas, and it supports local and edge-style hosting through Ollama and ONNX models such as Phi-3-mini. Where it is the best choice is in .NET applications that need structured, tool-using agents rather than a single prompt and response.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The learning curve is moderate and depends heavily on prior C# experience, since the examples, attributes and dependency injection patterns are idiomatic .NET. A developer should be comfortable with classes, attributes, async code and service registration before approaching plugins, because a plugin is created by defining a class and annotating its methods with the KernelFunction attribute, and plugins are designed to work with dependency injection for things like database connections and HTTP clients. No deep mathematics is required for the orchestration work, though understanding what a model can and cannot do helps when designing function descriptions. The official site is generous to beginners: it explains chat completion, walks through adding services, shows package installation commands for each provider, and gives concrete Docker and git commands for running Ollama and ONNX models locally. The main friction is conceptual rather than mathematical, particularly distinguishing auto function choice from auto function invocation, two settings that sound alike but control different things.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The connector ecosystem is broad. Official packages exist for Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, MistralAI, Google, Hugging Face, Azure AI Inference, Ollama, Amazon and ONNX, with Anthropic models reached through Amazon Bedrock. Providers that expose an OpenAI-compatible chat completion API, such as LLM Studio, can use the OpenAI connector. Documentation is substantial and page by page, covering function choice behaviours, function invocation, plugins, OpenAPI plugins, vector store serialization and chat completion setup. Community support follows the usual Microsoft open source pattern, with the GitHub repository as the centre of issues and contributions. One caveat visible throughout the material is maturity: the Mistral, Google, Hugging Face, Azure AI Inference, Ollama and Bedrock connectors are all marked experimental and require suppressing the SKEXP0070 warning, and the vector store serialization page is marked as preview.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Semantic Kernel serves both ends of that spectrum, but not identically. For prototyping, adding a chat completion service takes a few lines, auto function calling is the default, and plugins can be imported from native code, a URL, a file or a stream, which makes a working agent quick to assemble. For production, the framework exposes controls that matter: manual function invocation returns chosen functions to the caller instead of executing them, parallel function calling can run sequentially by default or concurrently by setting AllowConcurrentInvocation, and parallel calling can be disabled entirely with the OpenAI or Azure OpenAI connector. Direct serialization for vector stores gives full control over how models map to database schemas and is described as the best route to performance, at the cost of being specific to one data store. The price of this range is configuration complexity and a moving surface, since several connectors remain experimental and preview features may change.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The facts and the official site support a picture of an actively maintained Microsoft project with a large GitHub following and first-party documentation, which suggests real use in .NET shops building AI features. The documentation names OpenAI, Google, Mistral, Facebook, Amazon and others as chat completion providers, and it treats Semantic Kernel as the layer that simplifies function calling for applications. What the material does not provide is adoption numbers, customer stories or salary data, so any claim that it is an industry standard, or that it is legacy, would go beyond what is known. For someone choosing what to learn, the defensible reading is that it is a current, supported option with particular value if you work in C# and .NET, and less obviously relevant if your stack is elsewhere.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Semantic Kernel is primarily a C# framework, and its documentation also shows Python equivalents for several concepts, including function choice behaviours and the kernel_function decorator. It is typically used alongside .NET application code, dependency injection containers, HTTP clients and database connections, and it deliberately wraps rather than replaces the underlying model providers. The polyglot pattern it belongs to is the one where a host language orchestrates external AI services: the framework describes functions, the model chooses them, and the host executes them. Its OpenAPI plugin support is explicitly framed as a way to share plugins across different programming languages and platforms as an application matures, which places it in a mixed ecosystem rather than a single-language silo. The documentation notes that not all AI SDKs have an analogous plugin concept, since most offer only functions or tools.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The clearest limits are stated in the documentation itself. Function calling is supported by only a few AI connectors, and support among small language models is still limited. Several connectors are experimental and require warning suppression, and vector store serialization is in preview. OpenAPI support covers versions 2.0 and 3.0, with 3.1 handled by downgrading to 3.0, and operations with non-unique parameter names are skipped with a warning unless a workaround is applied. Existing specifications often need editing to be understandable to a model. Beyond that, the official material does not settle questions a team will ask: there is no guidance on benchmark performance, no cost analysis, no comparison with other orchestration frameworks, and no statement about long-term support timelines. Those gaps should be treated as open rather than assumed in either direction.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
